title: Latent-space projection coloured by physics: does the latent space organise by physics?
summary: A learned latent space is only useful if it is organised by something physical. Project it to two dimensions and colour each point by a known physical quantity: if the colour varies smoothly over the picture, the latent space has captured that quantity.

media.alt: Scatter of 700 points in a latent PC1 versus PC2 plane forming a horseshoe arch from lower left to the right, coloured by temperature from yellow (about 2100 K) at the lower left through teal to dark purple (about 900 K) at the right, with a colour bar labelled temperature T in K.
media.caption: Reference render of class F6.10 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Does the latent space organise by physics?
read_the_figure.axes: x: latent principal component 1. y: latent principal component 2 (equal scale). Colour: temperature T in kelvin on a continuous scale (about 800 to 2200 K).
look_at: Does the colour change smoothly along the cloud, or is it mixed at random?
Is the structure one-dimensional (an arc or filament) or fills a region?
Where do neighbouring points have very different colours (folds, overlap)?
Is the colour variable named with its unit and is the projection stated?
as_drawn: 700 points lie on a horseshoe-shaped arc about 7 units long and roughly 0.3 thick, running from the lower left (hot, yellow, near 2100 K) over the top to the right (cold, purple, near 900 K).
Colour changes steadily along the arc; neighbouring points have similar temperatures (neighbours differ by about 27 K on average, random pairs by about 480 K).
The note says the picture is a 2-D projection of a learned latent state and that T varies smoothly along the manifold; the colour bar names the quantity and its unit.
At the hot end the arc turns downwards and the points spread over a wider range of PC1 (about -2.5 to -1.8).
read_the_figure.proves: A smooth colour field shows that the latent coordinates carry the information needed to order the data by that quantity. It does not prove the latent variable is physically meaningful in other respects, or that the projection preserves the true neighbourhoods.
if_wrong: Mixed colours: the latent space does not encode that quantity, or the 2-D projection discards the relevant direction.
Smooth colour but a horseshoe: a one-dimensional manifold often curls in PCA; the curl is a projection artefact, not physics.
No stated projection method: PCA, t-SNE and UMAP have different distortions and the reader cannot tell which applies.
must_check: colour = a physical quantity: the picture is a test of whether the latent space respects the physics, which is meaningless without a physical quantity in the colour.

terms.meaning: The lower-dimensional space in which a model represents its states.
A map of the latent vectors to two dimensions so they can be drawn.
A direction of largest variance of the data; PC1 captures the most variance, PC2 the next.
The share of the total variance carried by a component: its eigenvalue divided by the sum.
A low-dimensional curved surface (here a curve) on which the data lie.
How similar a physical quantity is between points that are close in the latent space.

remember: PCA: eigenvectors of the covariance matrix; explained variance = lambda_i / sum lambda.
Colour by a physical quantity, with a unit, on a perceptual scale.
A smooth colour field does not prove the latent space is physical; quantify it.
A horseshoe from PCA of a 1-D gradient is typical, not physical.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each point is one data state at its latent coordinates after projection to two dimensions. Position on the plane shows the relation of the latent vectors; colour shows the value of a physical quantity (temperature) on a continuous scale with a labelled colour bar. The aspect ratio is equal so that distances are not stretched.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: a learned latent space has no labels of its own. If you paint each point with a known physical value and see a smooth gradient, the model has arranged its states in an order that follows that value, so the physics is in there. If the colours are a patchwork, it is not. The picture is a quick, qualitative test of whether the learned representation is physically organised.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A 2-D projection throws away information: points that are far apart in the full latent space may overlap on the page and vice versa. Colour is one quantity; a space organised by temperature may be disorganised by composition. A smooth gradient can arise trivially if the quantity is the largest source of variance, as in PCA. Nonlinear projections (t-SNE, UMAP) can create or destroy clusters, and distances in them are not quantities.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Quantify the claim: regress the physical quantity on the latent vector and report R-squared, or measure the neighbour consistency as done above. Show several panels coloured by different quantities. A linear probe or a plot of the quantity against a single latent coordinate is a precise version.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a second panel coloured by a different quantity (a species fraction), print the explained variance ratios on the axes, and draw a thin grey line through the ordered points to show the manifold's path.

worked.title: Reading the latent map of the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What range of temperature does the cloud cover and how does it change along the arc? (2) Is the structure one-dimensional? (3) How would you turn the visual impression of smoothness into a number?

solution.text: (1) The colour bar runs from about 800 K (purple) to about 2200 K (yellow). Starting at the right-hand end (cold) and moving over the arc to the lower left the temperature rises steadily.
(2) The cloud is a thin arc: length about 7 units and thickness about 0.3, so it is close to a one-dimensional manifold with noise.
(3) Compare the temperature difference between neighbours with that between random pairs.

worked.answer: About 800 to 2200 K, rising from the right end to the lower left; essentially a curve of length 7 and thickness 0.3; neighbours differ by about 27 K against 476 K for random pairs, a ratio of 0.06.

analyze.q: At the hot end the points spread more. What could cause that?
analyze.hint: Noise, a fold, or a second variable.

evaluate.hint: Information versus meaning; other quantities; unseen conditions.

checks.q: Why colour the points by a physical quantity?
checks.hint: What does a latent space lack on its own?
checks.answer: A latent space has no labels; colouring by a known physical quantity tests whether its geometry follows that quantity.

checks.q: A covariance matrix has eigenvalues 3 and 1. What fraction of the variance does PC1 carry?
The projection is a clean horseshoe with smooth colour. Give one reason to be careful before concluding that the latent space is one-dimensional and physical.
checks.answer: The horseshoe may be an artefact of the projection (PCA curls one-dimensional gradients), and neighbours in the picture may not be neighbours in the full latent space; verify with the neighbour-consistency ratio in the full space and with other colourings.
